newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FEATURE - Taiwan steel firms look for greener pasture abroad.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Taiwan steel firms look for greener pasture abroad.

text.p: For years, Taiwan's strapping steel firms have feasted on the island's huge market that came with soaring economic growth.
Now, these companies are learning that the grass may be greener elsewhere.

Citing scarce land, expensive labour and a lack of natural resources, steel makers are looking to China, East Asia and Australia in search of what analysts call the "last paradise" of world steel industry.

"It is absolutely vital before the year 2000 to transfer some of the downstream processing and production to China and East Asian countries, due to the adverse investment environment back home," said Kuo Kin-mao, head of Taiwan's steel industry association.
Kuo predicted that with rapid industrialisation, East Asia alone will demand about 45 million tonnes of imported crude steel per year by 2000, sharply up from the current 15 million tonnes.
China's annual demand for imported steel is expected to remain stable at 15 million tonnes, he added.

"The entire world steel industry is looking at China and East Asia, because they are expected to have the fastest economic growth into the next century," said Paul Huang, vice president of marketing for Taiwan's biggest steel firm, China Steel.
By the turn of the century, Taiwan's market, despite a hefty annual consumption of 22 million tonnes, may become so saturated that local firms are forced to branch out.

Domestic steel makers currently supply about 12 million tonnes a year for Taiwan's market, with China Steel alone churning out 5.65 million. Several more plants are being built that may double the output by 2000.
Heeding this inevitable oversupply, several makers already are looking outward.

Earlier this year, private upstart An Feng group went ahead of longtime state-backed China Steel to land Taiwan's first major overseas steel project, signing a US$1.2 billion deal to build a slab mill in Western Australia.
An Feng said its project with Australia's Kingstream Resources, set to produce 2.4 million tonnes of slab a year, would integrate its steel production.
"We now have to rely on imported slabs for our downstream products, but imported slabs are inconsistent in price and supply," An Feng president Chu An-hsiung told Reuters.
"When the slab plant is finished, we will be able to supply our own upstream materials and we won't have to buy raw material from abroad," Chu said in an interview.
He said his company's move "Down Under" may prompt others to follow.
"Before no one stepped outside. Now that we've stepped out, there are bound to be a lot of others who follow if our project proceeds smoothly," he said.
Both China Steel, privatised in 1995 and among the world's 20 largest steel firms, and Kuei Yu Industrial Corp are mulling to build plants in Australia.
But despite its abundant supply of iron ore, Australia lacks a major market for steel products, and analysts said firms will turn to China and East Asia once they exhaust Taiwan's market.
"China and East Asian countries may be the last paradise for steel industry," said China Steel's Huang.
Two more domestic projects to upgrade production already are under way, intensifying the industry's need to find a broader market to prevent oversupply.
China Steel will complete a fourth steel plant by June 1997 to increase its annual output to 8.05 million tonnes.
Yieh Loong Co Ltd also plans a T$114 billion (US$4.15 billion) plant with an annual capacity of 7.5 million tonnes, expected to be completed by 2001.
Taiwan's steel makers currently export only 10 percent of their products; by 2000 they would have to ship out 20 to 30 percent, Kuo estimated.

A crucial factor affecting overseas markets is whether China maintains its huge 15 million-tonne annual demand for imported steel. Some experts fear that China's booming steel industry eventually would produce so much steel that it not only becomes self-sufficient, but cuts into other markets as well.

"Everyone is talking about this concern. But steel is not just a matter of quantity, but also quality and processing. No one country can make every kind of steel product by itself," said Chen Yuan-chung, executive vice president for China Steel.
"With increasing liberalisation which results in a free market, the competition will be on who can make better and cheaper steel," Chen added.
But even if China maintains a market for importers, many Taiwan companies are reluctant to invest in the mainland because of political and social concerns.

"A steel project is one which you have to invest a lot of time and money, and the return takes a long time. Therefore you have to be very careful when considering investments under an unstable atmosphere," Chen said.

"China is still a semi-closed society, with personal relations still holding sway over law. It is some way off from being a modernised country, so I personally feel it is not the time to invest there now," said An Feng's Chu.
Despite the present obstacles, the steel association predicted that companies eventually would warm up to China out of sheer economic interest.
"Just imagine this difference: China's annual per capital consumption of steel right now is 85 kg (187 pounds) per year, and Taiwan's is over 1,000 kg (2,200 pounds)," Kuo said.
"This means China has huge room for development. There is the market if you can gain a competitive edge."
